text: Lithium Sulfur Batteries Very Important Paper Highly Solvating Electrolytes with Core-Shell Solvation Structure for Lean-Electrolyte Lithium-Sulfur Batteries Mengxue He, Lujun Zhu, Yatao Liu, Yongfeng Jia, Yizhou Hao, Guo Ye, Xufeng Hong, Zhitong Xiao, Yue Ma, Jianhao Chen, Muhammad Burhan Shafqat, and Quanquan Pang* Abstract: The practical energy density of lithium-sulfur batteries is limited by the low sulfur utilization at lean electrolyte conditions.

The highly solvating electrolytes (HSEs) promise to address the issue at harsh conditions, but the conflicting challenges of long-term stability of radical-mediated sulfur redox reactions (SRR) and the poor stability with lithium metal anode (LMA) have dimmed the efforts.
We now present a unique core–shell solvation structured HSE formulated with classical ether-based solvents and phosphoramide co-solvent.

The unique core–shell solvation structure features confinement of the phosphoramide in the first solvation shell, which prohibits severe contact reactions with LMA and endows prolonged stability for [S3] *� radical, favoring a rapid radical-mediated solution-based SRR.
The cell with the proposed electrolyte showing a high capacity of 864 mAhgsulfur � 1 under high sulfur loading of 5.5 mgsulfurcm� 2 and low E/S ratio of 4 μLmgsulfur � 1.
The strategy further enables steady cycling of a 2.71-A h pouch cell with a high specific energy of 307 Whkg� 1.

Our work highlights the fundamental chemical concept of tuning the solvation structure to simultaneously tame the SRR and LMA stability for metal-sulfur batteries wherein the electrode reactions are heavily coupled with electrolyte chemistry.

Introduction Lithium-sulfur (Li� S) batteries present an attractive alternative to the Li-ion batteries for next-generation energy storage, owed to the high theoretical specific energy and the high abundance of sulfur.[1] In the past decade, considerable efforts have been made in designing the cathodes with great success in the utilizable capacity and long-term stability,[2] for instance, by confining the sulfur/polysulfides in porous carbons or incorporating catalysts for the sulfur redox reactions (SRR).[3] However, it remains challenging to simultaneously achieve high specific energy and long cycling life to find its way as a practical battery chemistry.

This challenge lies on the low sulfur utilization and fast capacity fading at low electrolyte-to-sulfur ratios (E/S ratios).[4] In fact, achieving high sulfur utilization under lean electrolyte conditions (E/S5.0 μLmgsulfur � 1) in the conventional etherbased moderately solvating electrolytes (MSEs) has been intangible due to the low solubility and poor reactivity of lithium polysulfides (LiPSs) at such conditions, which is originated from the abruptly degraded transport and reaction kinetics of electrolytes with high-concentration (even saturated) LiPSs, and from the premature electrode passivation by the Li2S formation upon discharge.[5] Using sparingly solvating electrolytes (SSEs) can shift the sulfur reaction pathway from a dissolution–precipitation reaction to a quasi-solid-solid reaction.
The SSEs restrict polysulfide solvation, prevent shuttling and enable long cycle life at lean electrolyte conditions, but suffer from sluggish reaction kinetics.
Another effective strategy to facilitate the SRR under lean electrolyte conditions is to tailor the solvents’ molecular structure for regulating the speciation and increasing the solubility of LiPSs.

Solvents possessing a high Gutmann donor number (DN), including dimethylacetamide (DMA, 27.8 kcalmol� 1),[6] N-dimethylformamide (DMF, 26.6 kcalmol� 1),[7] dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 29.8 kcalmol� 1),[8] and 1,3-dimethyl-2-imidazolidinone (DMI, 29 kcalmol� 1),[9] have been shown to inherently promote LiPSs’ solubility compared to the low DN counterparts.[9–10] Specifically, these highly solvating electrolytes (HSEs) with high-DN solvents not only improve the solubility of LiPSs (and Li2S),[7,11] but also promote the formation of [S3] *� radicals during SRR, which appears to facilitate the conversion between long-chain and short-chain LiPSs.[12] Therefore, the HSEs are expected to enable formation of highly reactive LiPSs catholyte solutions during the reaction at lean electrolyte conditions, as opposed to the saturated and sluggish LiPSs catholyte solutions formed in conventional ether-based MSEs.
While with inherent promise to promote SRR at lean electrolyte conditions, the use of HSEs with high-DN solvents for Li� S batteries presents considerable practical challenges.

Further, the molecular mechanism affecting the formation and stability of radicals during the SRR remains unclear.

More critically, the stability with the lithium metal anodes (LMAs) imposes a conflicting requirement for the solvents, that is, the reactivity of solvents with LMAs increases significantly with the electron donicity, resulting in highly unstable interfaces and hence shortened cell life for HSEs with high-DN solvents.[13] Therefore, it is essential to design advanced electrolytes with regulated solvation structures which are compatible with LMAs while concurrently exhibiting the advantages of fast SRR kinetics for lean-electrolyte Li� S batteries.[14] In this study, we present a HSE featuring core–shell solvation structure which addresses the conflicting challenges by endowing both high stability for the [S3] *� radical and high electro(chemical) compatible with the LMA.

The electrolyte is composed of classical ether solvents and a high-DN hexamethylphosphotriamine (HMPA) co-solvent forming a core–shell solvation structure, wherein the HMPA is confined in the first-solvation shell via strong hydrogen bonding with ether solvents.
The confinement of HMPA leads to suppressed contact reactions with LMA at the interface and improved LMA plating efficiency.

Furthermore, the HMPA co-solvent inherently shows superior stability towards the highly reactive [S3] *�radical thereby activating a rapid radical-mediated solution-based SRR pathway and a 3D island-like Li2S deposition morphology, resulting high sulfur utilization at lean electrolyte condition.

The core–shell solvation structured electrolyte enables a high specific capacity of 864 mAhgsulfur � 1 with a low E/S ratio of 4.0 μLmgsulfur � 1 and a high sulfur loading of 5.5 mgsulfurcm� 2 at 0.1 C.
Notably, we demonstrate a 2.71-Ah Li� S pouch cell which delivers a high specific energy of 307 Whkg� 1 with stable cycling at 25°C.

Results and Discussion The Solvation Structure We hypothesize that the way to solve the conflicting challenges of promoting radical formation and compatibility with LMA essentially relies on manipulation of the solvation structure of the HSE.
The HMPA, with a high DN of 38.8 kcalmol� 1, is expected to exhibit strong solvation for the Li+ and hence to promote dissolution of LiPSs.
Furthermore, HMPA is a flame-retardant molecule which would add to the overall safety of the cell.

Therefore, we propose to use the HMPA as a co-solvent to the classical ether-based MSE, 0.5 M lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulphonyl)imide (LiTFSI) and 0.8 M lithium nitrate (LiNO3) in 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL), denoted as DD_HMPA.
A high LiNO3 concentration is used to further promote stable SEI and a low LiTFSI concentration is used to balance the electrolyte‘s physicochemical properties.
The classical DME/ DOL electrolyte (denoted as DD) was used as the base electrolyte for comparison.

Additionally, we studied another phosphoramide, tris(pyrrolidinophosphine) oxide (TPPO), and other classical high-DN solvents (DMSO and DMF) as co-solvent to the DD base electrolyte (denoted as DD_ TPPO, DD_DMSO, and DD_DMF, respectively) in an effort to explore the chemical features that determine the solvation structure, stability for the radicals and LMA stability of HSEs, which would provide theoretical guidance for designing high-performance HSEs.
The Li+-solvation structure of the DD_HMPA electrolyte was studied by 7Li nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and Raman spectroscopy.

Upon being added to the DD electrolyte, the 7Li NMR spectrum shows a gradual downfield shift as the HMPA volume ratio increases from 2% to 8%, reflecting a deshielding effect for Li+ due to solvation by HMPA (Figure 1a).[15] Additionally, the N� P� N bond in HMPA shifts from 629 cm� 1 to 643 cm� 1 in DD_HMPA with increasing volume ratios of HMPA as shown in the Raman spectroscopy,[16] indicating the change of HMPA environment, that is, its participation in Li+-solvation (Figure S1).

Notably, the HMPA molecule exhibits significant solventsolvent intermolecular interactions with DME/DOL due to hydrogen bonding between the Hδ+ in HMPA and Oδ� in DME/DOL, evidenced by the downfield shift of the 1H NMR chemical shift at ~3.0 ppm for the DD_HMPA solvent (LiTFSI-free) compared to the pristine HMPA (Figure 1b).[17] Similar results are also observed for another phosphamide co-solvent, TPPO (Figure S2).

Instead, the 1H NMR spectra show an upfield shift for the DD_DMF and DD_DMSO solvents (LiTFSI free) respectively compared to the pure DMF and DMSO solvent (Figure 1c), opposite to the HMPA and TPPO solvents.

We hypothesize that this is due to the presence of other form of interactions between DME/DOL solvent with DMSO or DMF.[18] We performed ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations to understand the impact of HMPA on the Li+ -solvation structures from a molecular-to-mesoscale level.
The first solvation shell presents a large difference between the two electrolytes.

The radial distribution function (RDF) analyses (g(r) and coordination number, CN) show that in the base electrolyte, Li+ exclusively coordinates with about 4.5 O from the solvents (statistically 89% DME and 11% DOL) in the first solvation shell (Figure 1d).
For the DD_ HMPA electrolyte, we observe significant participance of HMPA in the first solvation shell (~0.5 O), other than the ~2.5 O from DOL/DME, owed to the strong solvating power of HMPA.

Surprisingly, we observe a fraction of O from the TFSI�anions in the first solvation shell of DD_HMPA which, based on the typical Li+-solvation complex shown in Figure 1e, is likely encouraged by the interactions between HMPA and TFSI� (between -N-CH3 and F3C-).

The second solvation shell presents an interesting difference—while in both electrolytes the second solvation shell comprises of the DME and DOL solvents with a fraction of the TFSI� anions, as signified by the increasing CN for O (in DME, DOL and TFSI� ) beyond r >4 Å (Figures 1d, e).

Indeed, the typical Li+-solvation complex clustering shown in Figure 1e supports this finding and shows the presence of the hydrogen bonding between the Hδ+ in HMPA and Oδ� in DME/ DOL.
These results clearly show the formation of a core– shell Li+ solvation structure wherein the inner core consists of HMPA/DOL/DME/TFSI� , and the outer shell consists of only DOL/DME/TFSI� .

The formation of intermolecular hydrogen bonding appears crucial in confining the reactive high-DN HMPA co-solvent in the first Li+ solvation shell and hence suppressing the side reactions with Li metal, as demonstrated with our assessment by directly reacting Li metal with the solvents.

While the pure HMPA solvent is highly reactive with Li metal forming dark blue products upon contact (Figure S3), upon being added to the DD base solvent with a volume ratio of 8%, none visible reaction with Li was observed over 7 days (Figure S3).
The suppressed side reaction with Li metal was also observed for DD_TPPO solvent.
In great contrast, the other high-DN solvents exhibit clearly side reactions with Li metal, signified by the dissolution (darkening) of Li metal and coloration of the solvents.

This suggests that the intermolecular hydrogen bonding between phosphamide groups with the DOL/DME plays a decisive role in stabilizing the interface with LMA; indeed, with the HMPA buried within the first solvation shell, their direct contact and reactions with the LMAs would be suppressed.

Formation of Polysulfides Free Radicals The speciation of LiPSs in the electrolyte is crucial for regulating the SRR pathway.

In particular, the trisulfide free radical [S3] *� is reported to be formed in high-DN solvents, which potentially acts as internal redox mediators to promote conversion kinetics between LiPSs and Li2S.[7,13a,19] As radicals tend to have rather short lifetime, one question to ask is how long would the formed radicals exist in the electrolyte?
One would expect that a longer presence of radicals would lead to a more pronounced redox mediating effect during the full cycle of the cell.
Another question is how does it depend on the chemical features of the electrolyte?
We now explore the behaviours of radicals in different solvents with dissolved Li2S6 using UV/Vis spectroscopy.

With 0.3 mM Li2S6 dissolved, in contrast to the yellowish solution for the DD base solvent indicative of nondissociated Sx 2� anions, the solutions of DD_HMPA appear blue and darker as the volume fraction of HMPA increases (Figure 2a, inset).
The UV/Vis spectra confirms strong presence of [S3] *�radicals at 617 nm in DD_HMPA solutions,[20] in addition to S6 2� and S4 2� (Figure 2a).

Upon immediate dissolving of 1 mM Li2S6, the [S3] *� /[S4] *�peaks in all high-DN solvents exhibit similar intensity, indicating similar concentrations of radicals at the original states (Figure 2b).

We observe that the intensity of S4 2� peak negatively correlates with that of the [S3] *� /[S4] *� peak, that is, the increase of one occurs with the decrease of the other, indicating an equilibrium reaction between S4 2�and [S3] *� /[S4] *� .
However, the long-term stability of the formed radicals is largely different in these high-DN solvents, which we propose is essential for mediating the SRR over the course of discharge/charge.

Specifically, after standing for 1 hour, while all solutions remains in ultramarine blue, the ones with DD_HMPA and DD_DMSO exhibit a higher [S3] *�concentration (UV/Vis intensity) than the other two (Figure 2c).

Over 24 hours standing, the concentration of radicals greatly decreases for all solutions due to the collision between the radicals (Figure 2d), as shown by the decreased intensity of the [S3] *� peak and colour fading of the solutions (Figure 2d, Figure S5).
However, the DD_ HMPA solution retains the highest concentration of the [S3] *� radical of all, and still shows a blue colour.
In contrast, the other solutions show almost absence of the [S3] *� peak, indicating the annihilation of free radicals.

We have carried out the density functional theory (DFT) calculations to examine the interaction between the high- DN solvents with Li-[S3] * or Li2S6 (Figure S6).
High-DN solvents exhibit higher binding energy with Li[S3] * primarily through solvent-Li+.
We understand that in the Li[S3] * or Li2S6, Li+ is a Lewis acid, and both [S3] *� and S6 2� are Lewis base and among the two, S6 2� is a stronger (harder) base than the [S3] *� .

According to the Pearson’s HSAB theory, we hypothesize that the higher-DN solvents show stronger solvent-Li+ binding, and therefore the formed solvent-Li+ complex shows weaker Lewis acidity (softer Lewis acid), which in turn shows stronger binding with the soft Lewis base [S3] *� .

For example, HMPA, showing higher binding energy with Li+ than other solvents, greatly reduces the acidity of Li+ in the solution, which stabilizes the [S3] *�radicals by forming stable HMPA� Li[S3] * complex.

The stabilized HMPA� Li[S3] * complex can prevent extensive colliding between [S3] *� free radicals, therefore prolonging their life time (Figure S6).[8,22] Further discussions are provided in Figure S6.

We therefore examined the nucleation and growth kinetics of Li2S in the differently regulated polysulfide/radical solutions with a LijLi2S6 cell using potentiostatic electrodeposition.
All cells were galvanicaly predischarged to 2.07 V at 0.05 C to remove all the long- chain LiPSs (Li2Sx, x>4), followed by a potentiostatic discharge at 2.02 V.
The current response at the voltage hold was recorded until the current dropped below 10� 5 A.
As shown in Figures 3a–c, the initial current drop results from the solution phase reduction of long-chain LiPSs to mid-chain LiPSs.
The subsequent current response reflects the nucleation and growth process of Li2S.

Specifically, the current increase indicates the expansion of the electroactive area due to either the increase in the number of Li2S or the nuclei growth of each Li2S nucleus on the electrode surface.[12b,23] Subsequently, the current decreases during the growth stage owing to the reduced active surface area from the deposited nuclei and the overlap of diffusion hemispheres.[12b,23] Additionally, the mechanism of Li2S electrodeposition in different electrolytes was elucidated by constructing dimensionless I/Im–T/Tm curves (Im: maximum current, Tm: specific time when the current reaches maximum) and comparing them with four classical electrodeposition models.
In the DD base electrolyte, the chronoamperogram curve shows a rapid current increase and decay, with a Li2S deposition capacity of only 353 mAhgsulfur � 1 (Figure 3a).

Notably, the Li2S deposition capacity significantly increases with the addition of high-DN co-solvent, reaching 618, 402, and 518 mAhgsulfur � 1 for DD_HMPA, DD_DMF, and DD_ TPPO electrolyte, respectively (Figures 3b, c, Figure S9a).

Furthermore, the Li2S deposition in the DD electrolyte follows a hybrid model between the two-dimensional instantaneous (2DI) and three-dimensional progressive (3DP) model (Figure 3a, inset) due to the enhanced Li2S solubility by the highly electron donating NO3 � , consistent with the observed smooth Li2S layer with scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging (Figure 3d).[8,12b] In this case, the subsequent growth of Li2S is controlled by the surface mass transport of electrodepositing species, and will consequently be impeded by the insulating Li2S layer.

In great contrast, the current response of the cell with the DD_HMPA electrolyte indicates a hybrid 3DP and 3DI (three-dimensional instantaneous) model, suggesting the Li2S growth is controlled by bulk diffusion and the HMPA facilitates a fast solution-mediated mechanism in SRR (Figure 3b, inset).

In fact, the [S3] *� radicals may act as a mediator to chemically react with deposited Li2S to form soluble short-chain Sx 2� , which essentially prevents premature electrode coverage with Li2S and hences the passivation.
Indeed, very small Li2S granules form on the electrode surface, consistent with a 3D Li2S growth mechanism (Figure 3e).

In the DD_DMF and DD_TPPO electrolyte, the Li2S deposition follows closely with the 3DI model (Figure 3c, Figure S9b), which indicates that rapid nucleation and growth produce large Li2S islands, which can hinder the bulk diffusion and continuous deposition (Figure 3f, Figure S9c).

The HMPA is shown to form hydrogen bonds with the DME/DOL solvents and is confined within the first solvation shell of Li+, thereby inhibiting the reaction with Li metal.
This unique solvation structure promotes long-term cycling stability of Li plating/ stripping by forming an inorganic-rich Li metal SEI (LiF, Li3N).

Additionally, HMPA, even at a lower volume fraction, can stabilize trisulfide radicals over an extended period of time, ensuring a solution-regulated reaction path and a 3D island-like Li2S deposition morphology for high sulfur utilization at low E/S ratios.

The developed electrolyte enables the cells to achieve a high capacity of 1213 mAhgsulfur � 1 at 0.05 C with an E/S ratio of 5.0 μLmgsulfur � 1 and 864 mAhg� 1 at 0.1 C with an E/S ratio of 4.0 μLmgsulfur � 1.

The 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME, purity > 99%) and 1,3-dioxolane (DOL, purity > 99.8%) were purchased from Macklin and MREDA, respectively.
The hexamethylphosphoramide (HMPA, 99%), dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, 99.9%) N, N-Dimethylformamide (DMF, 99.9%) and tris(pyrrolidinophosphine) oxide (TPPO, 98%) were acquired from Macklin.
Lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfony)-imide (LiTFSI, 99.5%) and lithium nitrate (LiNO3, 99%) were obtained from Aladdin.
All solvents were dried with activated molecular sieves (4 Å) for three days before using.
The LiTFSI and LiNO3 were dried for 48 hours under vacuum at 130 °C.
The electrolytes were prepared inside an argon-filled glovebox.
The base electrolyte was prepared by dissolving 0.5 M LiTFSI and 0.8 M LiNO3 in the DOL/DME mixed solvent (1:1, v/v, denoted as DD).
To prepare the DD_HMPA, DD_TPPO, DD_DMSO, and DD_DM electrolytes, the HMPA, TPPO, DMSO, and DMF were mixed with the base DD electrolyte with a volume fraction of 8% (unless stated otherwise).

The graphene/sulfur composite with sulfur loading of 80 wt% (G/S-80%) was prepared by melt diffusion method by mixing the graphene and sulfur powder at 155 °C for 12 hours.

The graphene used here was synthesized in a way according to our previous report.[1] The sulfur cathodes were prepared by casting the homogeneous slurry prepared from G/S, Super P, and polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) in an 8:1:1 weight ratio in N-Methylpyrrolidone (NMP) onto carbon-coated aluminum foils, followed by vacuum heating of the electrode at 60 °C for 12 hours.

The solvents interact with the Li2S6 primarily through solvent-Li+ bonding (Li+ is a Lewis acid).
The high-DN solvents generally show higher binding energies with Li+ than the DME or DOL does, indicating stronger solvent-Li+ interactions, which again leads to softer Lewis acidity for solvent-Li+.
Given that S62- is a harder Lewis base (than [S3]•−), the DME or DOL derived solvent-Li+ complex would form a stronger complex with S62- than the high-DN solvents do.

In contrast, the high-DN solvents show stronger solvent-Li+ binding than DME, and therefore the formed solvent-Li+ complex shows weaker Lewis acidity (softer Lewis acid), which in turn shows stronger binding with the soft Lewis base [S3]•- (S6 2- → 2[S3]•−).[7] This has been widely adopted to explain the stabilization of lithium superoxide LiO2 (Li+-O2-) over lithium peroxide Li2O2 (Li+-O22-) by using high-DN electrolyte solvents in Li-O2 batteries.[8] Note that O2- is a softer base than O22-.
Specifically, HMPA shows the stronger coordination with Li+ than DME or DOL does, resulting in a softer Lewis acid, which stabilizes the [S3]• radicals by forming stable HMPA-Li[S3]• complex.
The stabilized HMPA- Li[S3]• complex can prevent extensive colliding between [S3]• free radicals, therefore prolonging their life time.

These free radicals are present for a rather long period of time, which could facilitate the rapid reaction of sulfur at the initial stage.
Additionally, during the later stages, the [S3]•− radicals can readily accept electrons, and the products promote the further reduction of long-chain polysulfides to short-chain polysulfides.
